As he walked towards the door, the nephew looked at his uncle, but the look achieved nothing.

‘Good night!’ said the uncle. ‘I look forward to seeing you again in the morning. Sleep well! Take a light and show my nephew to his room! And burn him in his bed, if you please,’ he added to himself. Then he rang his small bell again and called his valet to his own bedroom.

After the valet had come and gone, the Marquis paced about in his loose dressing gown, gently preparing himself for sleep on that hot, still night. His clothes rustled, but his soft slippers made no sound against the floor. He moved like an elegant tiger. He resembled some wicked, unrepentant marquis in a fairy tale, enchanted to change into a tiger at intervals, with the transformation either beginning or just wearing off.

He crossed and recrossed his luxurious bedroom, watching fragments of the day’s journey return uninvited to his mind: the slow climb uphill at sunset, the sinking sun, the descent, the mill, the prison on its rocky height, the little village in the hollow, the peasants by the fountain, and the road worker in his blue cap pointing to the chain beneath the carriage. That fountain recalled the fountain in Paris, the small bundle on the step, the women bent over it, and the tall man raising his arms and crying, ‘Dead!’

‘I am cool now,’ the Marquis said, ‘and can go to bed.’

He left just one light burning on the wide hearth and let the thin gauze curtains fall around his bed. As he settled to sleep, he heard the night break its silence with a long sigh.

For three slow, heavy hours, the stone faces on the outside walls stared blindly into the darkness. For three hours the horses rattled their feeding racks, the dogs barked, and the owl made a sound very unlike the one human poets usually assign to owls. Such creatures stubbornly refuse to speak the lines written for them.

For three heavy hours, the carved faces of lions and people on the château gazed blindly into the night. Complete darkness covered the countryside, adding its silence to the muffling dust on every road. In the graveyard, the little mounds of poor grass could no longer be told apart. For all anyone could see, the figure on the Cross might have climbed down. In the village, both those who collected taxes and those who paid them slept deeply. Perhaps its thin inhabitants dreamed of banquets, as starving people often do, or of comfort and rest, as a driven slave or an ox under a yoke might dream. In their deep sleep they were fed and free.

‘That must have been the very period in Mr Elliot’s life that has always puzzled me,’ said Anne. ‘It must have been around the time he met my father and sister. I never knew him then; I only heard about him. But something about his behaviour towards them, and later about his marriage, has never fitted with the man I know today. He seemed to be quite a different person.’

‘I know all about it, all of it!’ Mrs Smith exclaimed. ‘He had met Sir Walter and your sister before I knew him, but I heard him talk about them constantly. I know they invited him and encouraged him to visit, and I know he chose not to go. I may be able to explain things you would never expect me to know. As for his marriage, I knew everything at the time. He told me every reason for and against it; I was the friend he trusted with his hopes and plans. I didn’t know his wife before they married—her lower place in society made that impossible. But I knew her throughout the rest of her life, or at least until its last two years, and can answer any questions you want to ask.’

‘No,’ said Anne, ‘there’s nothing particular I want to know about her. I’ve always understood that they weren’t happy together. But I would like to understand why, at that time, he was so unwilling to be friends with my father. My father certainly wanted to treat him with proper kindness and attention. Why did Mr Elliot pull away?’

‘At that stage of his life,’ Mrs Smith replied, ‘Mr Elliot had one aim: to make a fortune, and rather faster than he could by working in the law. He meant to achieve it by marriage. At the very least, he was determined not to ruin his chances by an unwise marriage. I know he believed your father and sister were inviting him and treating him kindly because they wanted the heir to marry the young lady. Whether he was right about that, of course, I can’t say. But such a marriage could never have given him the wealth and independence he wanted. I can assure you that was why he kept his distance. He told me the whole story; he hid nothing from me. It was strange that, just after leaving you in Bath, your cousin should become my first and closest new acquaintance when I married. Through him, I was always hearing about your father and sister.’

‘These were the events that weighed on Felix’s heart and made him, when I first saw him, the unhappiest member of his family. He could have borne poverty. Indeed, while it was the price of doing what was right, he took pride in it. But the Turk’s ingratitude and the loss of his beloved Safie were far more bitter misfortunes, beyond any remedy. Now the Arabian woman’s arrival brought his spirit back to life.

‘When word reached Leghorn that Felix had lost his wealth and social position, the merchant ordered his daughter to forget her lover and prepare to return to her own country. Safie’s generous nature rebelled against this command. She tried to reason with her father, but he left angrily, repeating his harsh order.

‘A few days later, the Turk came into his daughter’s room and hurriedly told her that he believed his hiding place in Leghorn had been discovered. He feared that he would soon be handed over to the French government. He had therefore hired a ship to take him to Constantinople and would sail in a few hours. He planned to leave her with a trusted servant. She could follow when she was ready, bringing most of his possessions, which had not yet reached Leghorn.

‘Once she was alone, Safie considered what she ought to do in this crisis. The thought of living in Turkey filled her with dread; both her religion and her personal feelings opposed it. Some of her father’s papers came into her hands, and from them she learned that her lover was in exile and discovered the name of the place where he lived. She hesitated for a while, but finally made her decision. Taking some jewels of her own and a sum of money, she left Italy for Germany with a servant. This young woman came from Leghorn but understood the everyday language spoken in Turkey.

‘Safie reached a town about twenty leagues from De Lacey’s cottage safely. There her servant became seriously ill. Safie cared for her with devoted affection, but the poor girl died. The Arabian was left alone, unable to speak the country’s language and knowing nothing of the ways of the world. Fortunately, she found herself among kind people. Before her death, the Italian servant had named their destination. The woman who owned the house where they had stayed then made sure that Safie reached her lover’s cottage safely.’
